steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on VertiBench, a benchmark for vertical federated learning that generates synthetic datasets with diverse feature distributions. Explain why evaluating VFL is hard with current real and synthetic datasets, why HFL benchmarks don't carry over, and summarize what VertiBench offers and our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Federated learning is known for making it possible to train models on distributed data with better privacy. In this study we look at vertical federated learning (VFL), which is less explored, where each party has a subset of the features. This matches a general definition of federated learning that includes privacy-preserving collaborative learning such as assisted learning and split learning. The VFL application is shown in Figure 1(a): there is first a development phase that uses synthetic or real-world benchmarks, and after validation it is deployed in actual federated environments.

It is hard to evaluate VFL algorithms because VFL data is inherently confidential. The scope of party imbalance and correlation that existing real VFL datasets cover, which we call the real scope, is limited. The datasets in the OARF benchmark, FedAds, NUS-WIDE, and Vehicle mostly represent scenarios where the parties are balanced and have weak correlations, as Figure 1(b) shows.

Because of the limits of the real scope, many VFL benchmarks use synthetic datasets. We call this evaluation scope the uniform scope. It represents the imbalance-correlation scope when the features are distributed equally among the parties, either randomly or manually. The uniform scope is commonly used in VFL experiments, but it limits the evaluation to scenarios where the parties are balanced and strongly correlated, according to Figure 1(b). Another critical limitation is that the uniform scope and the real scope do not align, which shows that a diverse and realistic VFL benchmark is really needed.

- HFL benchmarks
  - must pinpoint key factors affecting VFL algorithm performance
  - non-i.i.d. HFL benchmarks (e.g. NIID-Bench) fall short: assumptions on feature space + instance significance
  - HFL: independent, uniformly significant instances; VFL: features correlated, differing importance
  - HFL: all parties share feature space; conflicts with VFL's distributed features
  - -> unique analytical challenges for synthetic VFL benchmarks
- VertiBench
  - statistical analysis of supervised VFL tasks: party importance + correlation = two key factors
  - VertiBench: comprehensive VFL benchmark, novel feature-splitting methods
  - benefits: (1) encompasses uniform scope; (2) emulates real scope; (3) evaluates unexplored scenarios, e.g. imbalanced feature split
- Contributions
  - (1) synthetic dataset generation with varied party importance and correlation
  - (2) new real-world image-to-image VFL dataset Satellite
  - (3) evaluating party importance and correlation of real VFL datasets
  - (4) benchmarks of mainstream VFL algorithms; scalability; communication efficiency across imbalance levels
  - code on GitHub, splitting tools on PyPI, pre-split dataset available

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Federated learning is known for making it possible to train models on distributed data with better privacy. In this study we look at vertical federated learning (VFL), which is less explored, where each party has a subset of the features. This matches a general definition of federated learning that includes privacy-preserving collaborative learning such as assisted learning and split learning. The VFL application is shown in Figure 1(a): there is first a development phase that uses synthetic or real-world benchmarks, and after validation it is deployed in actual federated environments.

It is hard to evaluate VFL algorithms because VFL data is inherently confidential. The scope of party imbalance and correlation that existing real VFL datasets cover, which we call the real scope, is limited. The datasets in the OARF benchmark, FedAds, NUS-WIDE, and Vehicle mostly represent scenarios where the parties are balanced and have weak correlations, as Figure 1(b) shows.

Because of the limits of the real scope, many VFL benchmarks use synthetic datasets. We call this evaluation scope the uniform scope. It represents the imbalance-correlation scope when the features are distributed equally among the parties, either randomly or manually. The uniform scope is commonly used in VFL experiments, but it limits the evaluation to scenarios where the parties are balanced and strongly correlated, according to Figure 1(b). Another critical limitation is that the uniform scope and the real scope do not align, which shows that a diverse and realistic VFL benchmark is really needed.

To build a systematic synthetic VFL benchmark, we need to find the key factors that affect how VFL algorithms perform. Existing synthetic benchmarks for non-i.i.d. horizontal federated learning (HFL), like NIID-Bench, are not enough for VFL because of the assumptions they make about the feature space and instance significance. In particular, HFL benchmarks usually assume that instances are independent and equally significant, but this is not true in VFL where features have intrinsic correlations and different importances. Also, HFL benchmarks assume that all parties share the same feature space, which does not fit the distributed feature paradigm of VFL. So synthetic VFL benchmarks have their own unique analytical challenges.

Because of these limitations, we did a statistical analysis of supervised VFL tasks, and it identifies party importance and correlation as two crucial factors that influence the target probability distributions in synthetic VFL datasets derived from the same global dataset. Based on this, we propose VertiBench, a comprehensive VFL benchmark with new feature-splitting methods to generate synthetic datasets. VertiBench has three main benefits: (1) it generally encompasses the uniform scope; (2) it emulates the real scope effectively, which is shown by comparable performance on VertiBench-synthetic datasets; and (3) it makes it possible to evaluate other scenarios that previous studies have not explored, e.g. imbalanced feature split, which broadens the scope of VFL evaluation.

Our main contributions are: (1) Methods to generate synthetic datasets with varied party importance and correlation, which capture a broad scope of VFL scenarios. (2) Satellite, a new real-world image-to-image VFL dataset. (3) Techniques to evaluate the party importance and correlation of real-world VFL datasets, so that their feature split can be compared with synthetic VFL datasets. (4) Comprehensive benchmarks of mainstream cutting-edge VFL algorithms, which give key insights. For example, we show that VFL algorithms are scalable, which challenges earlier assumptions that VFL is difficult to scale, and we point out the challenges of communication efficiency in VFL datasets at different imbalance levels. The source code of VertiBench is available on GitHub, and the data splitting tools can be installed from PyPI. The pre-split dataset can also be accessed online.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Federated learning [1] is acknowledged for enabling model training on distributed data with enhanced privacy. In this study, we explore the less studied vertical federated learning (VFL), where each party holds a feature subset, in line with a general definition of federated learning [2] that includes privacy-preserving collaborative learning such as assisted learning [3] and split learning [4]. The VFL application, depicted in Figure 1(a), involves an initial development phase using synthetic or real-world benchmarks, followed by deployment in actual federated environments once validated.

Evaluating VFL algorithms is challenging because of the inherent confidentiality of VFL data [5]. The scope of party imbalance and correlation covered by existing real VFL datasets, termed the real scope, is limited. Datasets in the OARF benchmark [6], FedAds [7], NUS-WIDE [8], and Vehicle [9] mostly represent scenarios where parties are balanced and exhibit weak correlations, as depicted in Figure 1(b).

To address the constraints of the real scope, many VFL benchmarks [6,10,11] use synthetic datasets. This evaluation scope, termed the uniform scope, represents the imbalance-correlation scope under an equal distribution of features among parties, either random or manual. Although commonly adopted in VFL experiments [3,12], the uniform scope confines the evaluation to scenarios with balanced, strongly correlated parties according to Figure 1(b). Another critical limitation is the misalignment between the uniform scope and the real scope, which underscores the need for a diverse and realistic VFL benchmark.

Constructing a systematic synthetic VFL benchmark requires pinpointing the key factors that affect VFL algorithm performance. Existing synthetic benchmarks for non-i.i.d. horizontal federated learning (HFL), such as NIID-Bench [13], fall short for VFL due to their inherent assumptions about feature space and instance significance. Specifically, while HFL benchmarks typically assume independent and uniformly significant instances, this does not hold in VFL, where features exhibit intrinsic correlations and differing importances. Furthermore, HFL benchmarks assume that all parties share the same feature space, which is misaligned with VFL's distributed feature paradigm. This delineates the unique analytical challenges of synthetic VFL benchmarks.

Given these limitations, our statistical analysis of supervised VFL tasks identifies party importance and correlation as two crucial factors influencing the target probability distributions in synthetic VFL datasets derived from the same global dataset. Accordingly, we propose VertiBench, a comprehensive VFL benchmark with novel feature-splitting methods for generating synthetic datasets. VertiBench offers three primary benefits: (1) it generally encompasses the uniform scope; (2) it effectively emulates the real scope, as shown by comparable performance on VertiBench-synthetic datasets; and (3) it enables the evaluation of other scenarios not explored in previous studies, e.g. imbalanced feature split, broadening the scope of VFL evaluation.

Our primary contributions include: (1) Synthetic dataset generation methods with varied party importance and correlation, capturing a broad scope of VFL scenarios. (2) A novel real-world image-to-image VFL dataset, Satellite. (3) Techniques to evaluate the party importance and correlation of real-world VFL datasets, enabling comparison of their feature split with synthetic VFL datasets. (4) Comprehensive benchmarks of mainstream cutting-edge VFL algorithms that provide key insights. For example, we demonstrate the scalability of VFL algorithms, challenging prior assumptions about the difficulty of scaling VFL [6], and highlight the challenges of communication efficiency in VFL datasets across varying imbalance levels. The VertiBench source code is available on GitHub [14], and the data splitting tools can be installed from PyPI [15]. The pre-split dataset is accessible in [16].
